**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 51, verses 15–23:**

﴿Taking what their Lord gave them.﴾ Regarding this, there are two views:

First: it refers to the obligations (al-fara'id, the religious duties). This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

Second: it refers to the reward. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

﴿Indeed, they were before that doers of good.﴾ That is, before the obligations were prescribed, they were doers of good by responding (to the call). This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

Second: before the Day of Resurrection they were doers of good by fulfilling the obligations. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

﴿They used to sleep but little by night.﴾ Regarding this, there are two views:

First: it refers back to what came earlier, His saying ﴿Indeed, they were before that doers of good﴾. So ﴿they used to﴾ means that the doers of good were few. Then he began a new statement: ﴿but little of the night did they sleep﴾. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Second: it is a new address, begun after the completion of what preceded it, starting with ﴿they used to﴾ and so on.

Al-hujui (al-hujū') means sleep. The poet said:

*The spring rain renewed its meadow, removing you from it,*
*by a night when the eyes of people were in slumber.*

Regarding the interpretation of this, there are four views:

First: ﴿They used to sleep but little by night﴾ means they would awaken during it to pray and would sleep only a little. This is the view of al-Hasan.

Second: that some of them slept little for the sake of prayer at night, even though most of them slept much. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Third: that they were in a small part of the night when they slept, until they had performed the Maghrib and the 'Isha' prayers. This is the view of Abu Malik.

Fourth: that they used to sleep little, and "ma" is an extra, additional particle. This applies when the night prayer (qiyam al-layl) was obligatory.

(p. 366) Abu Dharr used to take hold of a staff and lean on it (during prayer) until the concession was revealed: ﴿Stand (for prayer) by night, except a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 2]. ﴿And in the hours before dawn they would seek forgiveness﴾. Regarding this, there are two views:

First: ﴿and in the hours before dawn they would pray﴾. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Second: they would delay seeking forgiveness for their sins until the pre-dawn hour, so that they might seek forgiveness at that time. This is the view of al-Hasan.

Ibn Zayd said: this is the time at which Ya'qub delayed seeking forgiveness for his sons, until he asked forgiveness for them at that time, when he said to them: ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord﴾ [Yusuf: 98]. Ibn Zayd said: al-sahar (the pre-dawn) is the last sixth of the night.

It was said that it was called sahar because it is ambiguous, lying between light and darkness.

﴿And in their wealth there was a right﴾. Regarding this, there are two views:

First: it is the zakat (obligatory alms). This is the view of Ibn Sirin, Qatada and Ibn Abi Maryam.

Second: it is a right other than zakat, by which one maintains ties of kinship, or feeds a guest, or carries the burden of another, or enriches the deprived. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

﴿For the beggar and the deprived.﴾ As for the beggar (al-sa'il), he is the one who asks people because of his poverty. As for the deprived (al-mahrum), there are eight views concerning him:

First: the one who abstains from asking people and does not make his need known. This is the view of Qatada.

Second: the one who comes after the spoils of war and has no share in them. This is the view of al-Hasan and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya.

It is related that "the Prophet (ﷺ) sent a military expedition, and they gained victory and took spoils. Then a people came after they had finished, and this verse was revealed."

Third: the one who has no share in Islam. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

Fourth: the impoverished one whose livelihood is hardly ever made easy for him. This is the view of Aisha.

Fifth: the one who seeks worldly things, and they turn away from him. This is also related from Ibn Abbas.

Sixth: the one who has been struck in his fruit and crops, and is helped by one who was not struck. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Seventh: the slave. This is the view of Abd al-Rahman ibn Humayd.

(p. 367) Eighth: the dog. It is related that Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz was on the road to Makkah when a dog came, so Umar tore off a shoulder of a sheep and threw it to the dog, saying: "They say it is the deprived one."

A ninth possibility is also admissible: the one whose maintenance is obligatory upon his kin, because he has been deprived of earning for himself, so that his maintenance became obligatory on the wealth of another.

﴿And on the earth are signs for those of certainty﴾, meaning admonitions for those among the people of certainty who take heed. In this there are two views:

First: what is in it of mountains, seas and rivers. This is the view of Muqatil.

Second: those nations of the past that He destroyed and the bygone generations that He annihilated. This is the view of al-Kalbi.

﴿And within yourselves. Will you not then see?﴾ Regarding this, there are five interpretations:

First: that it is the way of excrement and urine. This is the view of Ibn al-Zubayr and Mujahid.

Second: the proportion of the joints of your hands, feet and limbs is evidence that you were created to worship Him. This is the view of Qatada.

Third: in your creation from dust, and then behold, you are human beings dispersing. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Fourth: in your life and your death, and in what enters and leaves you of your food. This is the view of al-Suddi.

Fifth: in old age after youth, weakness after strength, and whiteness after blackness (of hair). This is the view of al-Hasan.

A sixth possibility is admissible: that it is the success of the incapable and the deprivation of the prudent.

﴿And in the heaven is your provision and that which you are promised.﴾ Regarding ﴿in the heaven is your provision﴾, there are two interpretations:

First: what descends from the sky of rain and snow, by which crops grow and creation lives, so it is their provision from the sky. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak.

Second: it means that your provision is from the presence of God, who is in the heaven.

(p. 368) A third possibility is admissible: in the heaven is the decree of your provision, and what He has apportioned for you is written in the Mother of Books.

As for His saying ﴿and that which you are promised﴾, there are three views:

First: of good and evil. This is the view of Mujahid.

Second: of Paradise and Hellfire. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Third: of the matter of the Hour. This is the view of al-Rabi'.

﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth, just as you speak.﴾ Regarding this, there are two views:

First: what the Messenger brought of religion and conveyed of message.

Second: what God enumerated for them in this surah of His signs and mentioned of His admonitions.

Al-Hasan said: It has reached me that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "May God destroy peoples to whom their Lord swore by Himself, and then they did not believe Him."

Qiss ibn Sa'ida, in his pre-Islamic time, used to alert his mind to these lessons, and so he took heed and learned. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I saw him on his camel at 'Ukaz, and he was saying: 'O people, listen and be aware! Whoever lives dies, whoever dies is gone, and everything that is coming is coming. What is the matter with me that I see people going away and not returning? Were they content with dwelling, so they dwelt? Or were they left alone, so they slept? Indeed, in the heaven there is news, and indeed, on the earth there are lessons: a raised ceiling, a laid-out night, seas that surge, and stars that set and then sink. I swear by God an oath in which there is no sin: indeed God has a religion that is more pleasing to Him than the religion you are upon.'"

Then he spoke verses of poetry, which I do not know. Abu Bakr said: I was present at that time, and the verses are with me, and he recited:

*Among the departed former generations, for us there are insights.*
*When I saw the watering places for death, having no return from them,*
*and I saw my people heading toward them,*
*the great and the small passing on,*
*the one who has passed does not return to me,*
*nor of those remaining is there one who will stay behind.*
*I became certain that I too will be going*
*to where the people have gone, a destination.*

(p. 369) The Prophet (ﷺ) then said: "He will be raised on the Day of Resurrection as a community alone."

We ask God Most High, together with the restrainer of reason and the deterrent of hearing, to turn away the impulses of desire and the occasions of trial.

There is no excuse after warning, and no pride after taking heed. And if you truly grasp guidance, you will attain from it success and honor.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 51, verse 24–30:

﴿Has there come to you the story of the honored guests of Abraham?﴾ ʿUthmān ibn Muḥsin said: They were four of the angels: Jibrīl (Gabriel), Mīkāʾīl (Michael), Isrāfīl (Israfil), and Rafāʾīl (Raphael).

Regarding His words ﴿honored﴾ there are two interpretations:

First: They are the ones who are magnified (muʿaẓẓamūn) in the sight of Allah.

Second: They are honored (mukramūn) because of Abraham's honoring them when he served them himself. This was said by Mujāhid.

ʿAṭāʾ said: When Abraham wanted to eat lunch or dinner, he would go out a mile, or two miles, or three, seeking someone to eat with him.

ʿIkrima said: Abraham was called Abū al-Ḍiyfān (father of guests), and his palace had four doors so that no one would pass him by.

The guest was called a ḍayf (guest) because he is "added" (uḍīfa) to you and lodged upon you.

﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace."﴾ Regarding this there are two interpretations:

First: This was said by al-Akhfash, meaning: "We come in peace, not as combatants," so that his soul would be at ease.

Second: That he invoked safety for them, and this is the view of the majority, because the greeting of peace implies tranquility and security. The poet said:

"Are you unjust, when your affliction is a man who offers the greeting of peace as a salutation, and is wronged?"

So Abraham answered their greeting of peace with its like: ﴿He said, "Peace, [you are] an unfamiliar people."﴾ Because he saw them in a form that was neither the form of humans nor the form of the angels he knew, so he did not recognize them, and said ﴿an unfamiliar people﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

First: That is, a people who are not known.

Second: That is, a people who cause fear; it is said "ankartuhu" when I feared him. The poet said:

"She disowned me, and what she disowned was nothing but the whitening hair and the bald head."

﴿Then he turned quietly to his family﴾: regarding this there are two interpretations:

First: He turned aside to his family, said by al-Zajjāj.

Second: He concealed his going to his family.

﴿Then he brought a fattened calf﴾. As for the calf, regarding its being so named there are two interpretations:

First: Because the Children of Israel hastened (ʿajjalū) in worshipping it.

Second: Because he hastened (ʿajjala) in following his mother.

Qatādah said: He brought them a calf because most of Abraham's property was cattle, and he chose for them a fattened one as an increase in honoring them; and he brought it roasted, and this is omitted from the speech because of the indication in it.

ʿAwn ibn Abī Shaddād narrated that Jibrīl touched the calf with his wing, and it got up running until it reached its mother, and the mother of the calf was in the house.

﴿Then he brought it near to them, and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ Because they refrained from eating, since the angels do not eat or drink. Makḥūl narrated that they said: "We will not eat it except for a price." He said: "Eat, for it has a price." They said: "And what is its price?" He said: "When you put your hands [to it], that you say: 'In the name of Allah,' and when you finish, that you say: 'Praise be to Allah.'" They said: "With this Allah has chosen you, O Abraham."

﴿So he sensed fear of them﴾ because they did not eat; he feared that their coming to him was for an evil they intended against him.

﴿They said, "Fear not," and gave him the good news of a learned boy﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

First: That he is Isḥāq from Sarah, citing His words in another verse: ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 112].

Second: That he is Ismāʿīl from Hājar, said by Mujāhid.

﴿ʿAlīm﴾ means that Allah will grant him knowledge when he grows up.

﴿Then his wife came forward in a ṣarrah﴾. Regarding this there are three sayings:

First: A cry and a moan, said by Qatādah, and from it is the poet's saying:

"And a draught of a drink without breath, in a ṣarrah of the scorching heat of summer."

Second: That it is a shout, said by Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid, and from it is derived the ṣarīr of the door, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"He overtook him with the swift ones, and behind him their sharp-edged ones in a ṣarrah that was not dispersed."

Third: That it is a group, said by Ibn Baḥr, and from it is the muṣarrāh of sheep, for the gathering of milk in its udder.

The bundle of dirhams was also called ṣurrah because of what is in it. The poet said:

"How many a youth has poured out, in his loins, the water of youth at the height of his vigor."

As for His words ﴿and she struck her face﴾, regarding it there are two sayings:

First: Its meaning is that she smeared her face, said by Ibn ʿAbbās.

Second: That she struck her forehead in astonishment.

﴿And she said, "[I am] a barren old woman!"﴾ That is: "Will an old barren woman give birth?" This was said by Mujāhid and al-Suddī.

Fifth: We are the possessors of abundance; nothing we wish for is ever constrained for us.
